metrics.title: Service testing
metrics.description: Builds tests that protect GATE services: policy, sessions, APIs, and regressions that would escape to Release Test.

levels.1: Adds tests only when asked; happy path only.
levels.2: Covers assigned changes including a few failure cases.
levels.3: Consistently tests business logic and error paths for owned services.
levels.4: Designs a test strategy for a complex GATE service or integration.
levels.5: Raises backend test confidence for the team (fewer escaped defects).
levels.6: Standardizes backend testing across GATE services.
levels.7: Sets organization-wide backend quality baseline for GATE.

metrics.title: Maintainable services
metrics.description: Writes backend code the next GATE engineer can change safely: clear structure, naming, and reviewable diffs.

levels.1: Code works with heavy guidance; hard to follow.
levels.2: Readable on small changes; larger diffs need cleanup in review.
levels.3: Produces review-friendly changes with coherent structure.
levels.4: Simplifies a messy GATE module without breaking behavior.
levels.5: Sets coding patterns others copy in backend reviews.
levels.6: Drives maintainability standards across services.

metrics.title: Data, logs, and state
metrics.description: Models GATE state so logs, sessions, config, and persistence stay consistent and queryable.

levels.1: Touches storage/logging with close review.
levels.2: Makes correct local changes; misses some integrity cases.
levels.3: Designs data/log changes that match how ops will query them.
levels.4: Evolves schemas or log contracts without silent breakage.
levels.5: Improves GATE observability data for several services.
levels.6: Sets data/log standards used across the product.
levels.7: Owns GATE data and telemetry strategy.

metrics.title: Service design
metrics.description: Designs GATE backend boundaries: APIs, policy evaluation, HA, and failure behavior.

levels.1: Implements a spec; does not yet propose design.
levels.2: Suggests small design tweaks on assigned work.
levels.3: Designs a feature-sized service change with trade-offs.
levels.4: Leads design for a complex GATE subsystem.
levels.5: Aligns backend design across multiple services.
levels.6: Sets architecture direction for GATE backend.

metrics.title: Production behavior
metrics.description: Ships backend changes that hold up under real GATE load, failover, and customer config.

levels.1: Production issues on owned changes are common.
levels.2: Most changes hold; misses some operational cases.
levels.3: Owned features behave in production as intended.
levels.4: Anticipates operational failure modes before release.
levels.5: Improves production resilience for a GATE area.
levels.6: Raises backend reliability across the product.

metrics.title: Backend diagnosis
metrics.description: Debugs GATE services with evidence: logs, traces, configs, and reproduction — not guess-and-patch.

levels.1: Needs a senior to find the root cause.
levels.2: Debugs with help; sometimes patches symptoms.
levels.3: Finds root cause on owned services and proves it.
levels.4: Diagnoses cross-service GATE failures.
levels.5: Teaches debugging patterns; shortens incident time.
levels.6: Improves how GATE diagnoses backend failures.
levels.7: Sets diagnosis practice for the product.

metrics.title: GATE UI quality
metrics.description: Builds admin and operator UI that is clear under real GATE workflows (policy, logs, status).

levels.1: Implements screens with heavy design/lead help.
levels.2: Delivers assigned screens; edge states are incomplete.
levels.3: Handles empty, error, loading, and permission states.
levels.4: Improves a complex GATE flow so operators make fewer mistakes.
levels.5: Raises UI consistency across GATE pages.
levels.6: Sets frontend UX patterns for the product.

metrics.title: State and data flow
metrics.description: Manages client state, API errors, and refresh so GATE UI stays truthful about device/system state.

levels.1: State bugs are frequent; needs pairing.
levels.2: Handles simple fetch/update; races still appear.
levels.3: Keeps UI state consistent with GATE APIs.
levels.4: Designs data flow for a complex console area.
levels.5: Simplifies shared frontend state for the team.
levels.6: Sets data-layer standards for GATE UI.

metrics.title: Usability
metrics.description: Makes GATE UI usable for operators: density, keyboard, contrast, and Persian/English where required.

levels.1: Visual only; usability issues ship unnoticed.
levels.2: Fixes obvious usability bugs when reported.
levels.3: Checks flows as an operator would, including errors.
levels.4: Removes a class of operator confusion in a module.
levels.5: Defines usability checks the team runs before PO Checking.
levels.6: Sets accessibility/usability bar for GATE UI.
levels.7: Owns GATE console usability at product level.

metrics.title: Frontend verification
metrics.description: Protects GATE UI with tests or disciplined manual scripts that catch regressions before Release Test.

levels.1: Relies entirely on others to find UI regressions.
levels.2: Checks happy path before handoff.
levels.3: Covers critical flows and obvious failure UI.
levels.4: Adds durable tests or checklists for a GATE module.
levels.5: Raises frontend catch-rate for the team.
levels.6: Standardizes frontend verification across the console.

metrics.title: UI performance
metrics.description: Keeps GATE consoles responsive on real data volumes (sessions, logs, policy lists).

levels.1: Performance issues ship unnoticed.
levels.2: Fixes slowness when someone reports it.
levels.3: Avoids obvious jank on owned pages.
levels.4: Profiles and fixes a heavy GATE view.
levels.5: Sets performance budgets for key screens.
levels.6: Improves performance patterns across the UI.

metrics.title: Frontend diagnosis
metrics.description: Finds whether a GATE console bug is UI, API, or product behavior — then proves it.

levels.1: Needs help to locate the layer at fault.
levels.2: Debugs with browser tools on assigned bugs.
levels.3: Isolates UI vs backend with evidence.
levels.4: Diagnoses tricky operator-only failures.
levels.5: Shortens UI incident time for the team.
levels.6: Improves frontend diagnosis practice.

metrics.title: CI/CD
metrics.description: Keeps GATE build, test, and package pipelines trustworthy and fast enough for the sprint cadence.

levels.1: Follows existing jobs; cannot yet change them safely.
levels.2: Fixes simple pipeline breaks with help.
levels.3: Owns pipeline changes for assigned GATE components.
levels.4: Improves pipeline reliability or feedback time.
levels.5: Raises CI quality used by several GATE tracks.
levels.6: Sets CI/CD standards for the product.

metrics.title: Release engineering
metrics.description: Produces GATE builds, artifacts, and version notes that QA and service can actually ship.

levels.1: Needs a checklist from someone else for every release.
levels.2: Runs a known release path with occasional misses.
levels.3: Executes GATE releases without drama for owned streams.
levels.4: Hardens release steps that previously failed.
levels.5: Makes multi-component GATE releases repeatable.
levels.6: Designs release process across versions.

metrics.title: Observability

levels.1: Uses existing dashboards only.
levels.2: Adds a metric or log when asked.
levels.3: Instruments owned systems so failures are obvious.
levels.4: Improves alert quality (less noise, faster signal).
levels.5: Builds observability that several roles rely on.
levels.6: Sets telemetry standards for GATE.

metrics.title: Environments
metrics.description: Keeps GATE lab, staging, and related environments close enough to reality to catch release risk.

levels.1: Uses environments; cannot repair them.
levels.2: Fixes simple env issues with help.
levels.3: Maintains environments needed for GATE sprint work.
levels.4: Removes a class of “works in lab only” failures.
levels.5: Designs env strategy for QA and service.
levels.6: Standardizes GATE environments across sites.

metrics.title: Pipeline and infra security
metrics.description: Protects GATE delivery: secrets, access, image/supply chain, and least privilege.

levels.1: Follows security rules when reminded.
levels.2: Handles secrets correctly on assigned work.
levels.3: Does not introduce obvious security gaps in pipelines.
levels.4: Closes a real pipeline or infra security gap.
levels.5: Raises security baseline for GATE delivery.
levels.6: Sets secure-delivery standards.

metrics.title: Operational response

levels.1: Escalates immediately without a first diagnosis.
levels.2: Restores service with help; weak write-up.
levels.3: Restores and documents a durable fix.
levels.4: Leads ops incidents that block the GATE board.
levels.5: Cuts repeat delivery-infra incidents.
levels.6: Improves GATE ops practice.

metrics.title: Network automation
metrics.description: Automates repeatable GATE/network work with scripts or APIs instead of one-off console clicks.

levels.1: Runs steps manually from a runbook.
levels.2: Writes small scripts for assigned tasks.
levels.3: Automates a real GATE/network workflow others reuse.
levels.4: Designs automation that survives device or API changes.
levels.5: Raises automation adoption on the team.
levels.6: Sets automation standards for GATE/network work.

metrics.title: Device and API integration
metrics.description: Integrates GATE with network platforms (REST, SSH, vendors) with clear contracts and failure handling.

levels.1: Calls APIs with heavy guidance.
levels.2: Implements a specified integration; error handling is thin.
levels.3: Builds a reliable integration with retries and clear errors.
levels.4: Designs a multi-device integration for GATE.
levels.5: Improves integration quality others depend on.
levels.6: Sets API integration patterns for the product.

metrics.title: Policy as code
metrics.description: Treats firewall/UTM policy and network intent as reviewable, testable change — not tribal knowledge.

levels.1: Applies policy changes by instruction only.
levels.2: Documents changes; little validation.
levels.3: Makes policy changes reviewable and reversible.
levels.4: Adds checks that catch dangerous policy diffs.
levels.5: Spreads policy-as-code practice on GATE.
levels.6: Sets policy-change standards across environments.

metrics.title: Network literacy
metrics.description: Reasons about L3–L7 behavior that APK Gate must inspect, NAT, route, or log.

levels.1: Needs a senior to interpret packet/path issues.
levels.2: Reads basic routing/firewall symptoms with help.
levels.3: Explains path, NAT, and policy hits for owned cases.
levels.4: Diagnoses non-obvious GATE/network interactions.
levels.5: Teaches network reasoning to software teammates.
levels.6: Sets the network bar for GATE engineers.

metrics.title: Tooling
metrics.description: Builds small internal tools that make GATE network work faster and safer.

levels.1: Uses tools others built.
levels.2: Patches a tool when asked.
levels.3: Ships a tool or script the team actually runs.
levels.4: Turns a painful workflow into a maintained tool.
levels.5: Portfolio of tools used across roles.
levels.6: Sets tooling standards and ownership.

metrics.title: Net + software diagnosis
metrics.description: Splits “device, path, GATE software, or config” and proves it with captures, logs, and diffs.

levels.1: Cannot yet isolate the layer.
levels.2: Debugs with help from service or backend.
levels.3: Produces a clear root-cause story on owned cases.
levels.4: Leads mixed net/software incidents.
levels.5: Shortens mean-time-to-diagnosis for the team.
levels.6: Improves GATE diagnosis playbooks.

metrics.title: Deployment
metrics.description: Installs and upgrades GATE in customer or lab topologies without avoidable downtime or leftover config debt.

levels.1: Follows a script; stalls on any deviation.
levels.2: Completes standard deploys; unusual topologies need help.
levels.3: Owns a deploy/upgrade including rollback plan.
levels.4: Handles messy real-world topologies cleanly.
levels.5: Improves deploy playbooks the team uses.
levels.6: Sets GATE deploy standards across sites.

metrics.title: Troubleshooting
metrics.description: Turns a customer or lab symptom into a GATE root cause using logs, policy, sessions, and topology.

levels.1: Collects info; diagnosis comes from someone else.

levels.3: Closes typical GATE cases with a clear write-up.
levels.4: Solves unusual multi-factor failures.
levels.5: Raises first-time-fix quality for the service track.
levels.6: Designs troubleshooting paths used by others.

levels.1: Configs work in the moment; later people cannot follow them.
levels.2: Documents the change; structure is inconsistent.
levels.3: Produces clean, named, supportable GATE configs.
levels.4: Repairs config debt that caused repeat tickets.
levels.5: Sets config patterns for common GATE designs.
levels.6: Standardizes configuration across customers/labs.

metrics.title: Customer communication

levels.1: Needs a lead on every customer thread.
levels.2: Updates when asked; tone is sometimes too internal.
levels.3: Gives timely, plain-language status and asks.
levels.4: Manages tense escalations without hiding risk.
levels.5: Improves how GATE service communicates as a group.
levels.6: Sets customer-comm standards with PO/support.

metrics.title: Escalation and knowledge

levels.1: Escalates with “it doesn’t work”.
levels.2: Includes logs; missing topology or repro.
levels.3: Sends a complete packet and tracks the answer.
levels.4: Turns escalations into team knowledge.
levels.5: Reduces repeat escalations in a GATE area.
levels.6: Designs the escalation path across roles.

metrics.title: Operational ownership
metrics.description: Stays with a GATE field issue through workaround, fix, and confirmation — not just the first reply.

levels.1: Hands off at the first hard step.
levels.2: Owns simple cases to close.
levels.3: Owns assigned cases through verification.
levels.4: Picks up aging GATE issues that threaten customers.
levels.5: Improves service SLA outcomes for the team.
levels.6: Sets operational ownership norms.
levels.7: Owns GATE service operations with leadership.

metrics.title: Test design
metrics.description: Designs GATE test coverage around risk: policy, HA, upgrade, logging, and operator paths — not only happy clicks.

levels.1: Executes cases others wrote.
levels.2: Adds cases for assigned features with help.
levels.3: Designs a feature test set that finds real defects.
levels.4: Designs risk-based coverage for a GATE area.
levels.5: Raises test design quality for the team.
levels.6: Sets GATE test-design standards.

metrics.title: Release Test
metrics.description: Runs GATE Release Test so the board gets a clear go/no-go, not a vague “still checking”.

levels.1: Needs a list for every pass; status is late.
levels.2: Completes a known suite; reporting is delayed.
levels.3: Finishes planned Release Test with a clear result.
levels.4: Shortens Release Test without losing signal.
levels.5: Makes Release Test a reliable GATE gate.
levels.6: Designs release-test strategy across versions.

metrics.title: Defect quality
metrics.description: Writes GATE bugs that developers can reproduce: build, topology, expected vs actual, evidence.

levels.1: Reports are incomplete; bounce in review.
levels.2: Most bugs are usable; some missing evidence.
levels.3: Defects are complete and correctly severity-tagged.
levels.4: Clusters defects so backend/frontend can see the pattern.
levels.5: Improves defect quality across the team.
levels.6: Sets defect standards used by service and QA.

metrics.title: Negative and security testing
metrics.description: Probes GATE the way a hostile or clumsy operator would: bad config, privilege, malformed traffic.

levels.1: Tests only the demonstrated happy path.
levels.2: Adds a few negative cases when reminded.
levels.3: Includes meaningful negative cases on owned features.
levels.4: Finds a class of abuse/misconfig bugs.
levels.5: Builds negative/security checks into the suite.
levels.6: Sets GATE negative-test standards.

metrics.title: Test automation
metrics.description: Automates stable GATE checks so humans spend time on exploratory and release risk.

levels.1: No automation yet.
levels.2: Extends existing automation with help.
levels.3: Adds reliable automated checks for owned areas.
levels.4: Turns a painful manual GATE suite into automation.
levels.5: Raises automation value for the whole team.
levels.6: Sets automation standards and ownership.

metrics.title: Risk communication
metrics.description: Tells PO and the lead what GATE can ship, what is unknown, and what would bite customers.

levels.1: Status is a list of cases, not a risk call.
levels.2: Flags obvious blockers late.
levels.3: Gives a clear risk summary with evidence.
levels.4: Changes the release call with a well-argued risk.
levels.5: Improves how GATE talks about quality risk.
levels.6: Sets go/no-go language with PO and lead.

metrics.title: Sprint reliability
metrics.description: Protects sprint goals with honest scope control and predictable finish quality on GATE work.

levels.1: Needs help to finish committed tickets inside the sprint.
levels.2: Usually finishes assigned work; flags slip risk late in the sprint.
levels.3: Holds commitments and splits or descope early when risk appears.
levels.4: Stabilizes sprint outcomes for a whole slice of the board.
levels.5: Raises the team’s planning honesty and finish rate across sprints.
levels.6: Sets planning norms used by more than one GATE track.
levels.7: Defines how GATE measures and protects delivery reliability.

metrics.title: Flow
metrics.description: Keeps work moving: limited WIP, fewer idle handoffs, faster feedback in Code Review and Release Test.

levels.1: Often waits on others without updating the ticket.
levels.2: Moves own tickets; still piles up WIP under pressure.
levels.3: Keeps personal WIP low and unblocks the next reviewer.
levels.4: Removes recurring wait time (review, test, deploy) for the team.
levels.5: Improves cross-role flow (dev → review → QA → PO).
levels.6: Designs process changes that cut GATE cycle time.
levels.7: Owns flow metrics and intervention for the product.

metrics.title: Blocker handling
metrics.description: Surfaces blockers with enough context for Technical Review, QA, or PO to act the same day.

levels.1: Blockers appear only when someone asks.
levels.2: Reports blockers in standup with partial context.
levels.3: Writes a clear blocker (impact, tried steps, ask) and follows through.
levels.4: Unblocks others and prevents the same stall from repeating.
levels.5: Builds a habit of early risk flags across the sprint.
levels.6: Changes how GATE tracks and clears systemic blockers.
levels.7: Sets the standard for risk communication on the product.

metrics.title: Definition of Done
metrics.description: Marks work done only when review, tests, and GATE acceptance checks are actually complete.

levels.1: Needs reminders before a ticket is truly done.
levels.2: Follows DoD on own tickets most of the time.
levels.3: Does not close work with known gaps in test or review.
levels.4: Holds peers to DoD in review and stand-up.
levels.5: Tightens DoD where GATE releases have been bitten.
levels.6: Aligns DoD across tracks (service, QA, product).
levels.7: Owns GATE done-criteria at product level.

metrics.title: Team process
metrics.description: Improves how GATE runs: retros, board hygiene, Original Story Point, and review queues.

levels.1: Attends ceremonies; rarely contributes changes.
levels.2: Gives useful retro notes on own work.
levels.3: Takes and finishes a process action item.
levels.4: Drives a practice change the team actually keeps.
levels.5: Improves a queue (Code Review, Technical Review, Release Test).
levels.6: Designs process used by multiple GATE roles.
levels.7: Sets GATE operating cadence with the lead and PO.

metrics.title: Task breakdown

levels.1: Needs a lead to slice the work.
levels.2: Breaks assigned stories into steps with help.
levels.3: Writes tickets others can pick up without a meeting.
levels.4: Slices risky GATE work so QA and PO can accept incrementally.
levels.5: Teaches others to break down ambiguous UTM/firewall work.
levels.6: Sets breakdown patterns for a subsystem.
levels.7: Defines how GATE scopes large product bets.

levels.1: Estimates are guesses; often far off.
levels.2: Estimates assigned work; updates late when surprised.
levels.3: Explains assumptions and revises when facts change.
levels.4: Improves team forecast quality on similar work.
levels.5: Accounts for cross-track dependencies in planning.
levels.6: Calibrates estimation across GATE roles.
levels.7: Owns how GATE forecasts major releases.

metrics.title: Communication
metrics.description: Writes and speaks so GATE teammates, QA, and PO can act without extra decoding.

levels.1: Updates are sparse or hard to follow.
levels.2: Communicates when asked; tickets sometimes lack context.
levels.3: Proactive, concise updates in Jira and chat.
levels.4: Frames issues so the next role can decide quickly.
levels.5: Improves how the team writes tickets and reviews.
levels.6: Aligns communication across GATE and adjacent teams.
levels.7: Sets the voice of GATE engineering with stakeholders.

metrics.title: Collaboration
metrics.description: Works with backend, frontend, DevOps, DevNet, service, and QA as one GATE delivery line.

levels.1: Stays in own lane; handoffs are rough.
levels.2: Cooperates when others reach out.
levels.3: Seeks the right teammate before the work stalls.
levels.4: Makes cross-role work smoother for everyone involved.
levels.5: Builds working agreements between tracks.
levels.6: Resolves recurring cross-team friction.
levels.7: Designs how GATE collaborates with other APK groups.

metrics.title: Ownership

levels.1: Drops work at the first handoff.
levels.2: Owns assigned tickets through coding, not always through verify.
levels.3: Follows work through review, test, and PO checking.
levels.4: Picks up orphaned GATE issues that threaten the sprint.
levels.5: Owns a subsystem’s health, not only tickets.
levels.6: Owns outcomes across several roles or releases.
levels.7: Owns GATE product health with the lead.

levels.1: Avoids feedback or takes it personally.
levels.2: Accepts feedback; rarely offers useful comments.
levels.3: Gives concrete, kind review notes and acts on received feedback.
levels.4: Raises the quality of team feedback loops.
levels.5: Coaches others on how to review GATE work.
levels.6: Builds a feedback culture across tracks.
levels.7: Sets calibration norms for GATE performance talks.

metrics.title: Mentoring

levels.2: Answers questions when asked.
levels.3: Pairs regularly and leaves notes others can reuse.
levels.4: Has a clear mentee or onboarding impact.
levels.5: Creates guides that shorten GATE ramp-up.
levels.6: Builds mentoring capacity in other seniors.

levels.2: Joins PO/support discussions with preparation.
levels.3: Handles routine stakeholder asks independently.
levels.4: Sets expectations and says no with a clear alternative.
levels.5: Represents GATE in cross-team forums.
levels.6: Shapes stakeholder process (intake, severity, SLA).
levels.7: Is a trusted face of GATE engineering externally.

levels.4: Steadies others during a bad release or outage.

levels.6: Improves how GATE handles high-severity events.

levels.7: Owns GATE talent development with leadership.

levels.summary: Works with close guidance on well-scoped GATE work. Learns product fundamentals and contributes safely. Impact is local and learning-driven.
promotionGates: Finish small, well-defined GATE tasks end-to-end with support
Follow team workflows: branches, reviews, and status updates in Jira
Raise blockers early with enough context for the next person
Document what you learned and apply review feedback
Show steady improvement across several sprints

levels.summary: Delivers well-defined work with moderate guidance and growing independence. Impact is consistent contribution to sprint goals.
promotionGates: Deliver well-defined work from planning to production with little rework
Work smoothly with QA, PO, and reviewers during a GATE sprint
Give review comments that catch real issues, not only style
Keep quality and delivery predictable across multiple sprints
Clarify requirements when a ticket is incomplete

levels.summary: Delivers independently across design, implementation, test, and release. Handles moderate ambiguity. Impact is reliable execution at team level.
promotionGates: Own features end-to-end with predictable quality and light oversight
Turn partially defined problems into a clear plan and a working change
Lead work that spans more than one sprint without dropping quality
Mentor newer teammates through pairing and review
Make technical choices and explain the trade-offs

levels.summary: Leads complex GATE decisions, reduces ambiguity, and raises team effectiveness. Impact is amplified through others.
promotionGates: Lead complex initiatives and cut delivery risk for the team

antiPatterns.title: Recency bias
antiPatterns.problem: Scoring only from the last sprint before review.
antiPatterns.fix: Use notes collected through the period, not memory of the last week.

antiPatterns.title: Velocity as a personal KPI
antiPatterns.problem: Treating story points as an individual score.
antiPatterns.fix: Velocity is a team planning tool. Score outcomes and quality, not raw points.

antiPatterns.title: Halo or horn
antiPatterns.problem: One strength or miss colors every domain.
antiPatterns.fix: Score each domain on its own evidence.

antiPatterns.title: Missing evidence
antiPatterns.problem: Scores of 4+ or 2- with no named example.
antiPatterns.fix: Tie outliers to a ticket, review, incident, or customer case.

antiPatterns.title: Gaming the metric
antiPatterns.problem: Optimizing the score instead of GATE outcomes.
antiPatterns.fix: Prefer cycle time, release health, and customer impact.

antiPatterns.title: Uncalibrated leads
antiPatterns.problem: Different reviewers using the 1–5 scale differently.
antiPatterns.fix: Calibrate once per cycle before scores are shared.

Receive lead recommendation and calibration based on evidence, not tenure
